evidence_quotes.quote: This scoping review aimed to explore the water, sanitation, and hygiene status in Zimbabwe and its influence on health outcomes.
Aligned with its main objective, the review seeks to answer the overarching research question: “What is the impact of WASH status on health outcomes in Zimbabwe?”
Studies focussing only on WASH access or conditions without linking to health outcomes
The distribution of the articles showed that 11 studies were conducted at the household level, 8 at the community level, and 1 at the individual level
the ongoing challenges within the Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH) sector suggest a weakened policy framework and its operationalisation.
However, the reviewed articles and other records call for urgent policy action, and there is a lack of discussion on how to implement these policies effectively.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household, school, and community water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) status and urban-rural disparities in drinking water and sanitation access in Zimbabwe (Tables 3 and 4).
criterion_notes.c2: Fails Criterion 2 under the active narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: the review does not analyse any rule-type legal, administrative, regulatory, or institutional mechanism governing service access (such as eligibility screening, documentation or tenure rules, tariff/cost-recovery rules, enforcement, or regulatory/utility ownership rules). Instead, the 20 synthesized empirical studies examine physical WASH infrastructure, environmental water contamination, climate hazards, and behavioural/clinical WASH-nutrition interventions affecting health outcomes. Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, although Table 2 lists WASH policy among broad background variables and a short narrative subsection on p. 13 ('Governance and Financial Constraints') notes weak policy operationalisation, high ZINWA bills despite water shortages, and underfunding of the Rural Water Information Management System (RWIMS), governance is treated only as unanalysed macro-governance background/recommendations rather than an empirical exposure linked to service access; thus the paper would also be excluded under the plain reading (especially given the absence of an analysed governance-to-access outcome relationship).
criterion_notes.c3: PRISMA-ScR scoping review systematically searching multiple databases up to 31 May 2024 (655 records screened; kappa = 0.85 on 20% dual screening) and synthesizing 20 peer-reviewed empirical studies (cross-sectional, cohort, case-control, geospatial, cluster-RCT, and qualitative) plus 10 national policy/survey documents.
criterion_notes.c4: The scoping review defines WASH status/access as the independent status/exposure variable and human health conditions (diarrhoea, cholera, typhoid, schistosomiasis, enteric dysfunction, child growth/development) as the study outcomes (Table 3), explicitly excluding studies that focus on WASH access without linking to health outcomes (Table 2). While Table 4 tabulates descriptive urban-rural WASH coverage gaps from national surveys, WASH service access is not evaluated as an outcome of a legal or governance exposure.
criterion_notes.c5: Population (urban and rural Zimbabwean households, communities, and individuals across 20 empirical studies and 10 national reports), exposure (WASH status, infrastructure, and behavioural/WASH interventions), outcome (WASH-related health outcomes), and study design (PRISMA-ScR scoping review) are clearly identifiable, though they do not form an eligible legal-exposure-to-service-access-outcome design.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is written in English.

study_design: Scoping review (PRISMA-ScR synthesis of 20 peer-reviewed empirical studies and 10 national policy/strategy/survey documents)
population_and_sample: Populations in rural and urban Zimbabwe across 20 peer-reviewed empirical studies (11 household-level, 8 community-level, 1 individual-level) and 10 national policy/survey reports selected from 655 records
exposure: Water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) status, infrastructure conditions, environmental contamination, and behavioural/clinical WASH interventions (e.g., pit latrines, handwashing, point-of-use water treatment, hygiene promotion)
outcome: WASH-related health outcomes (diarrhoeal diseases, cholera, typhoid, enteric infections, schistosomiasis, soil-transmitted helminths, child stunting/development, menstrual hygiene-related school distress), with national WASH access rates reported descriptively
rationale: Exclude (E03 - Wrong exposure). This PRISMA-ScR scoping review synthesizes 20 empirical studies and 10 national reports on the relationship between physical/behavioural WASH status or WASH-nutrition interventions (exposure) and infectious disease or child health outcomes (outcome) in Zimbabwe, explicitly excluding studies examining WASH access without health outcomes. It does not examine a rule-type legal, administrative, regulatory, or governance mechanism governing water or sanitation service access; brief mentions of weak policy operationalisation, ZINWA billing complaints, and RWIMS funding on p. 13 are unanalysed macro-governance background rather than an evaluated exposure linked to service access.
